title: Oil Just Had Its Worst Quarter Since COVID. India May Be the Biggest Winner.
excerpt: Brent crude crashed 43% from its April war peak to below $71 — erasing the entire Iran conflict premium and handing India a potential $30 billion annual import savings.
body:
It happened almost without anyone noticing. While the world obsessed over ceasefire language and toll threats in the Strait of Hormuz, crude oil quietly did something it hadn't done since the pandemic crashed demand in early 2020: it posted its steepest quarterly decline in six years.

Brent crude fell below $71 a barrel on Wednesday — down more than 43% from its April war-peak of $126.40 — after Qatar said indirect talks between the United States and Iran in Doha had produced "positive progress." The benchmark hasn't been this cheap since late February, days before the first American and Israeli strikes on Iran.

For India, which imports roughly 85% of the oil it consumes, this isn't just a market story. It's a potential economic turning point.

## The Numbers Behind the Crash

Oil's collapse has been staggering in both speed and scale. Brent has erased the entire geopolitical risk premium that accumulated during the four-month U.S.-Iran conflict, and analysts are now cutting their price forecasts for the first time since the war began.

A Reuters poll of 31 economists published this week projects Brent will average $84.50 per barrel in 2026 — down from $90.44 forecast just a month ago. West Texas Intermediate is expected to average $79.49, compared with last month's projection of $84.63. Some bearish forecasters see prices grinding toward the mid-$60s if the Strait of Hormuz fully normalises.

"There's more optimism as more oil goes through the Strait of Hormuz," said Phil Flynn, senior analyst at Price Futures Group. "The market is signalling that once we get past this, the gloves are going to come off and we're going to probably produce more oil in the world than we ever have."

Vice President JD Vance said oil flows through the waterway had returned to pre-war levels, though he didn't cite figures. Tanker data tells a more cautious story — traffic has recovered but remains patchy, and freight rates through the strait are still elevated.



> **""There's more optimism as more oil goes through the Strait of Hormuz," said Phil Flynn, senior analyst at Price Futures Group."**


## What It Means for India

Every dollar drop in crude saves India roughly $2 billion a year on its import bill. At current prices, the savings from the peak are staggering: a $55 per barrel decline from April's highs translates into potential annual savings north of $30 billion — money that would otherwise drain out of the economy to pay oil producers.

The impact is already showing. India's current account deficit, which had widened sharply during the war months as oil costs surged, is set to narrow significantly. The rupee, which came under intense pressure when Brent crossed $120, has stabilised. And inflation expectations — a critical variable for the Reserve Bank of India's interest rate decisions — have begun to ease.

"The combination of lower crude, rupee stability and measures to draw foreign inflows has improved sentiment and liquidity," said Ajit Banerjee, president and chief investment officer at Shriram Life Insurance.

Indian equity markets reflected the optimism. The Nifty 50 gained 0.59% on Wednesday to close above 24,000. Banking stocks led the charge, with June gains of over 6% for the sector. The market has now posted monthly gains for three consecutive weeks.


## The Hormuz Variable

The oil crash is built on a single, fragile assumption: that the Strait of Hormuz will stay open.

U.S. and Iranian negotiators spent two days in Doha discussing maritime traffic in the strait and unfreezing Iranian funds — the two most contentious issues under June's interim agreement. Qatar's foreign ministry called the talks productive, but neither side said whether they had bridged their differences.

The next meeting won't take place until after the funeral of Iran's late Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, who is due to be buried on July 9. That leaves at least a week of diplomatic silence — and Iran has repeatedly said it will begin charging tolls on ships passing through the strait in mid-August, once a toll-free grace period expires.

"Hormuz continues to reopen but it's patchy, unpredictable, and not fully transparent," said Vandana Hari, founder of oil market analysis provider Vanda Insights.

If talks break down and Iran reasserts control over the strait, analysts warn prices could snap back toward $80 and beyond. Depleted global inventories — at their lowest since 2003 — leave no cushion to absorb a fresh disruption.

## The Bigger Picture

Beyond the immediate Hormuz dynamic, structural forces are weighing on oil. Morgan Stanley now models a global oil surplus of 4.8 million barrels per day in 2027. Chinese demand has softened. And the flood of returning supply — from Iranian, Russian, and OPEC+ barrels — is overwhelming what remains of the war premium.

For India, the risk calculus has shifted. The country's October decision to dramatically increase Russian oil imports — now accounting for more than half of all imports — looks increasingly like a hedge that paid off. Russian crude trades at a discount to Brent, meaning India's effective import cost is even lower than the headline price suggests.

Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman is expected to factor lower oil prices into the revised fiscal estimates when she presents the Union Budget later this month. Lower import costs free up fiscal room that could go toward infrastructure spending, rural programmes, or subsidies — a decision the diaspora will watch closely, given its implications for investment returns and family support costs.

For now, the market is betting on peace. Whether that bet holds depends on a funeral in Tehran, a toll booth in the Hormuz, and a set of negotiators who haven't yet agreed on what they already agreed to.
